description: We’re a passionate team of builders and problem-solvers tackling astronaut health monitoring for long-duration space missions. Combining software engineering, data science, and human-centered design, we’re creating an intuitive platform that turns physiological and behavioral indicators into clear, actionable alerts for crews in deep space.
summary: ZeroG Pulse is a health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long missions, where a message to the flight surgeon takes minutes each way and can be lost in a blackout. The crew measures a vital sign (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, SpO2, sleep, mood, stress or radiation dose). One Rust engine judges it against ranges for the environment it was taken in, tags the NASA Human Research Program hazards behind it, and places it on a four-step ladder: Monitor, Self-care, Consult ground, Urgent. A clickable body view shows status as colour, icon and word. Guidance offers only actions the onboard kit allows. When ground is needed, the app drafts an SBAR report and sends it over a delayed link, and keeps working offline. If the rich interface fails, a plain safe-mode console shows the same status from the same event log, so no two screens can disagree. Every range states whether it is adapted from NASA numbers or our own placeholder, and all crew readings are simulated. On the way to Mars, the crew has to judge their own health; ZeroG Pulse gives them a clear answer and a next step.
details:
What it does

ZeroG Pulse helps astronauts answer two questions without waiting for Earth: is this number a problem, and what do I do now? Deep-space crews face the five hazards NASA's Human Research Program names: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment. Near Mars a message to the flight surgeon takes minutes each way, so the crew must measure, judge and act on their own.

How it works

1. A body view opens on the crew's status. Today's checks flag what is due, for example a stale blood pressure reading.

2. A guided card explains how to measure in space and why it matters there. The astronaut enters the value; every reading carries its environment, device and confidence.

3. One deterministic Rust engine assesses it: a low-confidence reading never raises an alarm, and an out-of-range one is placed on a four-step ladder (Monitor, Self-care, Consult ground, Urgent). Two trusted out-of-range readings in a row escalate to Consult ground.

4. "Why?" explains the range, what is expected in flight and the source behind it, with a tag saying whether the range is adapted from NASA numbers or a placeholder.

5. Guidance offers only actions the onboard kit allows. When ground is needed, the app drafts an SBAR report (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) and sends it over a delayed link; the reply comes back after the same delay, and the outbox waits through blackouts.

6. If the rich interface is lost, a plain safe-mode console shows the same status and accepts readings, because every screen derives its view from the same append-only event log.

7. An activity-only crew score (streaks, XP) rewards doing checks without ever showing health values.

Benefits and impact

For the crew: a clear status and next step without medical training. For flight surgeons: structured SBAR reports, sent only when the ladder says ground is needed. For the mission: one engine, so the rich app, safe mode and ground can never disagree, and the tool keeps working when the screen or the link fails. On Earth, the same pattern fits remote clinics, ships and polar stations where a doctor is hours away.

Tools and languages

Rust (core engine, compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen), TypeScript with React and Vite (crew and ground web app, inline SVG body view), egui (safe-mode console, native and WebAssembly), axum (Ground Station API, JSONL storage), Tauri (desktop app), an Android WebView shell, GitHub Actions and Cloudflare Pages for CI and deployment.

What makes it creative

Status is computed once, in one engine, and every face renders what it says, so a reading entered in safe mode appears in the crew app and the reverse. The delayed ground loop is built in, not bolted on. The hazard lens ties every indicator to the NASA hazard that drives it.

What we considered

Honesty: all crew readings are simulated, never called NASA data, and every range shows its source status. No NASA document we found gives numeric in-flight vital-sign ranges, so we say so per indicator: sleep and radiation dose are adapted from NASA numbers; the rest are our own placeholders with NASA context. Safety: no diagnoses and no medication doses; ZeroG Pulse is not a medical device. Accessibility: status is always colour plus icon plus word. Resilience: the crew app and safe mode work fully offline.

Team: Tarek Darwish, Mostafa Emad El Din, Amr Yasser, Sama Waheed, Mohamed Naser.
